doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: The blues, swing and what counts as jazz
title: Kenny G and what counts as jazz
summary: Thomas and Rowe agree Kenny G plays instrumental pop, comparing him to Herb Alpert.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You’re doing yourself a large disservice.

Absolutely. And a disservice to a public who may not know jazz history. And if you are either calling yourself a jazz musician or allowing yourself, because you are an instrumentalist say, to actually be called a jazz musician and you’re not that — Kenny G is not a jazz musician. I’m not saying Kenny G can’t play. Kenny G has a nice tone on the soprano sax, and I don’t mean to just — you know there’s a group of people who just knee jerk condemnation of certain people and Kenny G is one of them. But I’m using him as an example. He plays instrumental pop and instrumental R&B. Let’s call it what it is. There’s a market for that obviously.
Herb Alpert. When I was a kid he was, and in fact I read a fact recently that Kenny G surpassed Herb Alpert as the largest selling instrumentalist. But Herb Alpert, no one
called him a jazz musician. He was playing instrumental pop music and it was very pleasant and stuff. So let’s just call Kenny G an instrumental pop musician.
